title: Arrest, Denial, and Trial Before Pilate
overview: Jesus is arrested in a garden, questioned by the high priest's family while Peter denies knowing him, and handed to the Roman governor Pilate, who finds no crime but faces a crowd demanding another prisoner.

parts.label: Arrest in the garden (vv. 1-11)
parts.note: Jesus goes to a place Judas knows well and steps forward to meet the soldiers rather than hide; his words "I am he" can also be read "I am," echoing how God names himself, which John seems to signal when the arresting party falls back. He makes sure his friends go free, stops Peter's sword, and calls his coming suffering a "cup" from the Father that he chooses to drink.

parts.label: Taken to Annas first (vv. 12-14)
parts.note: Annas was a former high priest who still held great influence, and his son-in-law Caiaphas held the office that year. John reminds readers that Caiaphas had earlier said it was better for one man to die for the people, which John reads as an unintended prediction of Jesus' death for others.

parts.label: Peter denies Jesus (vv. 15-18, 25-27)
parts.note: Peter, who had just drawn a sword for Jesus, now three times denies even being his follower, and the rooster's crow fulfills what Jesus had told him would happen. The other disciple who got Peter into the courtyard is unnamed; many think it was John, but this is uncertain.

parts.label: Questioned by the high priest (vv. 19-24)
parts.note: Jesus says he taught openly, so the fair way to judge him is to ask those who heard him, as a proper hearing would call witnesses. For saying this he is slapped, and he calmly asks what he said that was wrong.

parts.label: Handed over to Pilate (vv. 28-32)
parts.note: The leaders would not enter the Roman governor's residence because doing so would make them ritually unclean and unable to eat the Passover meal. Under Roman rule they could not carry out an execution themselves (historians debate the exact limits), and a Roman death meant crucifixion, the "lifted up" death Jesus had spoken of.

parts.label: "My kingdom is not of this world" (vv. 33-40)
parts.note: Pilate wants to know if Jesus is a rebel king, and Jesus answers that his rule does not come from earthly power and does not use force, since his followers are not fighting. Pilate finds no charge and offers a customary Passover release, known only from the Gospels, but the crowd chooses Barabbas, a man linked to violent revolt.

disagreement: Christians differ on what "my kingdom is not of this world" means: some take it to mean Jesus' rule is mainly spiritual or in the life to come, while others read it as a different kind of rule, one that refuses force but is meant to reshape life and society now.
think: Pilate asks "What is truth?" When have you found it hardest to tell what was true, and what helped you decide?
